paragraphs.text: Training-data attribution is typically validated against content-similarity proxies rather than causal effects known in advance. In this exploratory factory-farming study with Qwen3-4B, the same premise specification produced installed effects spanning a 22x range: +0.1574 for short answers versus +0.0072 for long articles at two epochs. Length, premise density, and voice differed across this pair, the long endpoint rose at three epochs, and separately estimated factorial corpus arms provided the clean decomposition of length and density. We installed per-source effects by fine-tuning, measured each against a retrained control, removed each method’s top-ranked documents, and retrained. Paired seeds were used only for declared seed-paired families; single-seed and separately configured readings remained labeled separately, with checkpoint details retained in provenance.

paragraphs.text: The headline result was counterproductive attribution: at the ten-percent budget, TracIn’s attributable fraction was -0.91 at seed 42 and -0.42 at seed 7, with both intervals excluding zero, because removing its top-ranked documents increased the installed effect. This sign test against zero was independent of the overlap criterion, and the evaluated implementation used gradient agreement at a single final checkpoint. By contrast, at the twenty-percent budget, oracle removal recovered +0.52 and +0.62 of the installed effect across the two seeds, with both intervals excluding zero. This recorded positive control was not a candidate attribution method; in these cells, the installed effect was removable and the instrument detected removal.

paragraphs.text: The resulting benchmark asks whether document rankings recover a known, removable training effect rather than merely retrieve similar content. The positive-control contrast showed that removal by separately measured effect eliminated roughly half the installed effect across both seeds, with both intervals excluding zero; this was a recorded positive control rather than a candidate attribution method, and in these cells the instrument detected that the installed effect was removable. By contrast, removing documents ranked highest by TracIn increased the installed effect at both seeds, with both intervals excluding zero. This sign test against zero does not depend on the overlap criterion, and the evaluated implementation uses gradient agreement at a single final checkpoint.

paragraphs.text: At the narrower removal budget, the oracle readings pointed in opposite directions across seeds while both intervals included zero. This power-diagnostic reading does not order those cells against the wider-budget cells. More broadly, the oracle’s overlap with the word-count baseline suggests that, at these interval widths, the overlap criterion has limited resolving power; a narrow-budget overlap verdict therefore says little about method quality. That conclusion interprets the overlap table rather than measuring diagnostic power and does not extend to the design’s overall diagnostic power.

paragraphs.text: Every replication claim in the seed-paired contrasts is bounded by two training seeds. Two draws leave the source of the delta-predictability disagreement unresolved; the opposing seed-specific directions are not characterized as noise.

The design cannot exclude the possibility that perturbing the corpus at all moves a small quantity; doing so would require a dose-matched random-removal arm retrained with the same full fine-tuning procedure. The single-final-checkpoint gradient-agreement formulation also represents only one attribution estimand. Summing gradient agreement along the training trajectory would be expected to score differently, but that comparison lies outside this evaluation.

By contrast, at the narrower budget, removal guided by the single-final-checkpoint TracIn implementation evaluated here increased the installed effect at both seeds.
